newsitem.title: UK: US, Europe funds up foreign holdings - report.
newsitem.headline: US, Europe funds up foreign holdings - report.

text.p: U.S. investor holdings of international stocks surged to $480.7 billion in 1996, a gain of 37 percent, a report on global investment flows from fund data company Technimetrics said.
Total holdings of international equities by European institutional mutual funds climbed $68.6 billion in 1996, a gain of 28.2 percent, the report said.
In the fourth quarter U.S. equity investments pushed upward by $3.8 billion, with gains in Europe and Latin America but declines in Canadian and Asia-Pacific equities.

"The rise in the market value of U.S. international investments was remarkably stronger in 1996 than 1995. Considering the strength of the U.S. stock market in 1995, the strong surge in foreign investment by U.S. institutions a year later is hardly surprising" the report said.
The search for diversification by U.S. investors benefited European companies, the report said, with U.S. ownership of European stocks growing $7.4 billion in the fourth quarter.

The value of U.S. institutional investments in Asia-Pacific equity issues plunged more than $6 billion in the fourth quarter, driven down by falls in the Tokyo and Hong Kong bourses as well as weakness in the Japanese yen.

European institutional mutual funds saw their holdings grow by $10.4 billion in the fourth quarter alone. Investment within Europe was behind most of the rise, with holdings in European cross border securities or non-domestic European equities accounting for 82 percent of the increase.
The report said European ownership of U.S. equities increased by just $0.8 billion in the quarter, reflecting the continuing underweight stance of European institutional investors in U.S. equities.

Asia-Pacific regional share of total European international investment slumped to 26.7 percent at the end of 1996 from 29.1 percent at the end of 1995. This continues a fall from a 33.1 percent peak in 1994.
Likewise, U.S. ownership of Asia-Pacific stocks fell by $6 billion in the fourth quarter to $100.6 billion, the report said.

"Part of the reason for the overall decline in the Asia-Pacific allocation by European and U.S. investors has been the lacklustre performance of Japan, which represents a large share of the Asia-Pacific market" the report said. - London newsroom, +171 542 2734
